newsitem.title: USA: Judge says plaintiffs can see Liggett paper.
newsitem.headline: Judge says plaintiffs can see Liggett paper.

text.p: A Mississippi judge ruled on Wednesday that internal documents from Brooke Group Ltd's Liggett Group could be turned over to plaintiffs in a $650 million second-hand smoke lawsuit against the U.S. tobacco industry.

In a ruling that could set an important precedent for anti-tobacco cases across the country, Jones County Circuit Judge Billy Joe Landrum granted plaintiffs' attorneys access to 11 documents as part of a case brought by the family of the late Burl Butler, a barber who died of cancer in 1994.

The family contends that the 60-year-old Butler, who never smoked, died from the second-hand smoke he breathed from the cigarettes, cigars and pipes of people who patronized his Laurel, Miss., barber shop over the course of 30 years.
In recent days, the case has come to be seen by legal experts as a first test for whether or not the Liggett documents can be used in lawsuits against the industry.

The documents were part of last week's settlement between the fifth largest U.S. cigarette maker and 22 state attorneys general. The states are suing the industry for an estimated $30 billion in Medicaid funds spent treating poor smokers.
In response to a motion from plaintiff's attorneys, Landrum ruled 11 Liggett documents were not "privileged" and therefore could be turned over to attorneys for the Butler family.
But he also stayed the order until Friday to give tobacco industry lawyers a chance to appeal his ruling to the Mississippi Supreme Court. They indicated that they will.
"This is pretty historic. There's no question in my mind that these documents are going to see the light of day," said state Attorney General Mike Moore, who attended the hearing.
Landrum, who broke away from the hearing for more than an hour to read the Liggett documents, later described their contents as part of trial preparation.

"Portions of these documents deal with expert opinions and testimony of experts employed in anticipation of litigation who were not expected to be called as witnesses at trial and are discoverable," the judge said in his ruling.

Ron Motley, a plaintiffs' attorney from Charleston, S.C., later said he believed the documents would show that cigarette makers destroyed papers to hide information both from other plaintiffs and from the public.
Tobacco attorney asked the court to delay the ruling until the defendants had been given a chance to review the documents.

"Your honor, we haven't seen that. We can't respond," a lawyer for R.J. Reynolds told Landrum after the judge had read the documents. "We came here today on very short notice to consider whether the court was going to review certain documents en camera. Somewhere along the line, we have lost."
Landrum ordered that copies of the documents be forwarded under seal to Jackson County Chancery Court Judge Wiilliam Myers in Pascagoula, Miss.
Myers is presiding over Mississippi's legal effort to recoup nearly $1 billion Medicaid funds from cigarette makers.
Landrum also set out a system by which tobacco industry lawyers would be able to review five boxes of Liggett documents not covered by his ruling.
